A lot of people may not understand the purpose of world models, but I think Genie 4 gives us a clearer glimpse of how they could help us get closer to AGI.

Google is already combining Genie with Gemini (unfortunately, 3.8 Flash in the live loop). Gemini can watch the simulation, break goals down into simpler steps and adjust its plan as the world changes.

Eventually, pairing an LLM’s reasoning with a world model’s learned physical dynamics could give agents a way to test actions and improve their spatiotemporal reasoning. Similar to how humans can imagine a real world scenario and think through what might happen before doing something.

This gives agents a place to compare actions and learn from simulated outcomes before trying them in the real world, assuming the simulations are accurate enough.

I think this could help with some of the spatial and physical reasoning problems models still struggle with. Humans can mentally rehearse what they’re about to do. But LLMs are only able to do text based reasoning and can describe physics and math possibilities, in text, but an interactive world model gives AI a way to play them out.

The physics and long-term consistency still need work, obviously, but this is a great step toward giving AI richer environments to interact with and learn from.

For anyone using Grok Bot or Claude to make video edits, there are a few things nobody seems to be doing.

This is a small clip from an upcoming video of mine.

FIXES: graphics pinned to the screen instead of the scene, dark scenes that break into bands and blocks on X and YouTube, numbers that jiggle while they count, and soft shots that don't match the rest of the edit.

👾Graphics pinned to the screen instead of the scene

The top half of this video has its graphics pinned to the screen the way most edits do, and the bottom half has them locked to the world.

When the camera moves, a label that points at something stays where it was and the picture slides out from under it. NASA Ames tested this with pilots in 1995. Landing in a simulator, they took 2.5 seconds longer to react to a plane on the runway when their flight symbols were on the head-up display instead of the instrument panel. Their explanation was that symbols on the glass don't move the way the world outside does, and that difference pulls attention onto them. Their fix was to draw the symbols as objects in the world so they move with it, and pilots flew their path more accurately.

In an edit, that means tracking how the background moves in each shot, ignoring the people in it, and moving every graphic that points at something along with the camera. A label on a target follows the target, and titles and counters stay fixed.

👾Dark scenes that break into bands and blocks on X and YouTube:

X and YouTube compress what you upload, and the smooth gradients in dark footage turn into bands and blocks. The fix is to smooth those gradients before the grain goes on.

👾Numbers that jiggle while they count:

Counters jiggle because the digits in a lot of fonts are different widths, so the number shifts sideways as it counts. Putting each digit in a fixed-width slot keeps it still.

👾Soft shots that don't match the rest of the edit:

Measure the sharpness of every shot too. The softest one stands out next to the shots around it, and that's the one to regenerate.

Big win for local LLM inference!

This open-source engine generates tokens 2.7x faster than Ollama on a MacBook:

I tested it on a base M5 MacBook Pro with Qwen3.5 4B at 4-bit and the same 9.2k-token prompt. Ollama ran its MTP build, so both had speculative decoding.

- Prefill: Ollama 464 tok/s, Magnitude 755 tok/s (1.6x)
- Decode: Ollama 22.6 tok/s, Magnitude 60.0 tok/s (2.7x)
- End to end, Magnitude finished in half the time

The video below shows both runs side by side.

The Ollama numbers don’t mean it’s badly built. Its kernels were simply tuned in advance.

A kernel is the small GPU program behind every matrix multiply and attention step. Its speed depends on choices like how work is split across GPU cores and how data moves through memory.

The best choices change with every chip. Apple Silicon alone spans 8 to 80 GPU cores and under 70 to over 800 GB/s of bandwidth, and every model has its own layer sizes.

A prebuilt engine has to pick one set of settings for all of them, so most local setups run on a compromise.

Magnitude replaces that compromise with tuning on your machine:

↳ When you download a model, it compiles that model’s kernels locally.

↳ It tries different kernel configurations and keeps whichever runs fastest on your chip.

↳ It pairs each model with the fastest speculative decoding drafter it has found, so each pass of the model produces more than one token.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/gpwU34NFlw

(don’t forget to star it 🌟)

This matters most for agents. Every file and tool output has to be processed before the model writes anything, and that prefill step is where kernel efficiency shows up. Concurrent sessions also share prefix caches, so parallel agents don’t slow each other down.

Magnitude is an open-source (Apache 2.0) inference engine written in Rust. It plugs into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and other agents with one click.

I shared the GitHub repo above.

HOLY F*CK. I made an 8K photoreal rock + moss material from a single reference with Claude Opus 5.5

No scanner. No paid library. Just a reference, an image generator, Python scripts and Blender.

The pipeline:
1. Generated the base texture from a reference (top-down, flat light, no shadows)
2. Built every PBR map from it: roughness, AO, normal, 16-bit displacement
3. Aligned all maps to the diffuse, so color, height and normals sit in the exact same place
4. Pulled a moss mask out of the diffuse color
5. Claude wrote the Blender scripts: material, scene, lights, this poster

8192×4572. Real displacement in Cycles, not a fake bump.

The trick that makes it look real: moss is NOT the same material as rock.
Rock: roughness straight from the map.
Moss: roughness 1.0, soft sheen, subsurface, its own height in little cushions.
Two materials inside one shader.

Where I messed up:
- first sphere looked like plastic. Low-poly mesh + weak displacement = nothing moves. Fix: dense mesh, real displacement
- moss height turned into needles. Fix: two masks, a sharp one for shading and a blurred one for height
- plane at displacement 0.40 = stretched spikes. Dropped it to 0.12

Can AI do “taste”?

For a while now, whenever I have a few tokens left over, I’ve been trying to teach “my Claude” “taste”.
Technically, what I’m after is being able to set any design task (from a landing page to a poster) and get back a graphically interesting result in a particular style that is defined, but not down to the last detail.
The challenging part: unlike code, whose correctness, maintainability and vulnerability are measurable, or at least validatable and optimizable, “taste” works in a far more diffuse way.

To make it even harder, the target style is supposed to deliberately work with breaks that, judged purely “objectively”, could be rated as mistakes. At the very least it should be as far away as possible from the “conventionally pretty” of the usual.

Much like in language, where a particular style or a sense of humor always lives in the break with the “usual”, not in perfect mastery of it (even if today’s culture machine absorbs the “break” into the norm faster than an Insta reel is forgotten).

Why all this:
AI is capable of producing perfect-looking UI, at least for the web, when:

it’s left completely free and is allowed/asked to work out its own style from nothing but a briefing (at first glance the results here are often impressive)
it’s asked to copy a style 1:1 or follow a detailed branding manual

It “fails”, in very clear quotation marks, when it comes to grasping a “style” on a somewhat more abstract level and deriving something new from it. That’s my impression at least, and it applies to language as well as to graphic output.
Some will interject: “Yet.” And anyway: what does it matter if the two cases above work?

Well, my impression so far is simply that the field in the middle, the field of the “vague idea”, is exactly the interesting one. It’s the field where we need to check whether AI will eventually take over here too, in what I’ll call the creative field. We also need to check how far along it is, and whether (or where) it helps or maybe even gets in the way.

In all of this, I’m less interested in proving one thing or the other. I’m more interested in finding the altitude at which a creative process has to take place (and graphics are basically just a cipher for a whole range of knowledge and creative work). At that altitude, what comes out at the end isn’t arbitrary and doesn’t scream AI smell. Instead, it a) understands what is one’s own and then b) transfers it to situations that weren’t named beforehand.

Thought further, this leads straight back to the very concrete: what does an optimal interface for working with AI look like?

Attached is a little sampler of the iterations and test-results so far.

My conclusion so far: it is at the very least extremely hard, and I don’t dare speak of success, not even remotely.

If you think your technical skills are becoming useless because AI can write code, I think you're seriously underestimating what's coming.

I've been reading how engineers at top AI companies are working with coding agents. And honestly, it's making me rethink where I should invest my time as an engineer.

Here are 5 things I'm personally focusing on:

1. Getting much better at codebase design. If you can read a 17,000-line file and reduce the input tokens needed for the same AI coding task by 83%. That's fascinating because good architecture now directly affects how efficiently your agents can work.

2. Developing deeper domain expertise,  an agent can write a payment integration, but knowing how settlement, refunds, retries and reconciliation should behave is a different matter. You want to understand the business well enough to catch mistakes that perfectly valid code can still make.

3. LGetting better results from smaller models. I know Opus 5.5 makes everyone feel powerful, but here's a more interesting challenge. Can you get a cheaper model like Terra or Haiku to complete the same task reliably? Learning how to achieve that consistently is a skill I'd love to get better at.

4. Making my systems easier for agents to inspect. OpenAI gave its coding agents access to running applications, browser interactions, logs and traces. That way, agents could actually reproduce bugs and verify their fixes. I'm particularly interested in building more of this into my own workflows.

5. Understanding where the next engineering bottleneck appears. Anthropic went from roughly 2,500 to over 30,000 code changes merged daily. Suddenly, source control, builds and CI became major problems. I think there's a huge opportunity for engineers who can identify and solve these problems as AI increases development speed.

The more I read about how these teams are working, the more I realize how much there is for experienced engineers to explore.

Personally, I don't want to spend the next few years just getting faster at prompting AI to write code. We need to understand these systems well enough to make a smaller team capable of doing work that previously needed dozens of engineers.

I'm considering writing a detailed article on these ideas, with real engineering examples and things you can try yourself.

<inputs>
Ask me for: my video idea (one line is fine), the setting, the length (60-90 s) and the narrator (an ElevenLabs voice, or "free" for a local text-to-speech). Everything is built in code: no AI images, no AI video. Make it MY story, not a copy of an example.
</inputs>

<format>
The style is a second-person survival thriller with stickmen, built as a series:
- "Imagine you…" hook with a time stamp in the first 3 s
- a HUD with the DAY number and a clock that moves forward through the episode
- 3-4 RULES, each one paid off on screen
- a threat that escalates and is mostly shown, not told
- a twist that makes one rule impossible
- a two-choice ending ("DO YOU OPEN IT?" style, a green and a red option, "COMMENT BELOW") and "FOLLOW FOR DAY 2"
Around 20-30 voice lines, 60-90 s, a new shot every 1.5-3 s.
</format>

<story>
Write a beat sheet and the script first and show me both before building anything.
- One line = one visual. Rules are short commands.
- Open a new question every ~10 s and only answer it with a bigger one.
- Put the viewer in POV for the scary parts: what you see through a door, a window, a phone, a peephole.
- The ending is a choice where both options look bad.
- Write numbers twice: the caption form ("11:58 PM") and the spoken form ("eleven fifty-eight P M") for the text-to-speech.
- Rotate settings between episodes (apartment, subway, school at night, hospital, cabin, plane, office, motel) and fit the threat to the setting.
</story>

<look>
Pick a palette per story, but keep the language:
- real 3D low-poly sets with real lights and shadows; the mood comes from light (one warm practical, one cold fill, one strong accent such as a door gap, a screen or a siren)
- the stickman is flat and 2D-looking: a light body with a thick dark outline, round strokes, dot eyes, no mouth; give the main character one mark (a scar, a cap, a colour) so doubles and callbacks read
- the overlay: a monospace HUD top-left, chunky captions (1-3 words, key words in an accent colour), a tilted rule sticker with a big condensed title, phone screens drawn in 2D
- banned: AI frames, glossy 3D characters, emojis, music with vocals, long captions
</look>

<shots>
A library to adapt to the story (never use all of them):
- the opener: a camera move that starts tight on you and pulls out to show where you are
- POV phone in your hands (2D phone UI, two stick thumbs)
- a macro on the one detail that matters
- outside chaos from above (balcony, bridge, window): physics vehicles, a running crowd, something collapsing or burning
- third-person action in the room: walking with planted feet, reaching, hesitating, barricading
- POV interaction: throwing, holding a torch, opening something
- a close-up of your face for the reaction
- a low angle on a door or vent: light leaking in, shadows moving
- knocks, shakes, things falling
- a fisheye peephole, camera or window view of the threat stepping closer
- the choice screen and the end card
</shots>

<tools>
What each tool is for. Install whatever is missing, and ask me before anything paid:
- three . js: the 3D engine; it runs inside a web page. Download its module file locally so renders don't depend on the internet. Use its post-processing passes for bloom, plus one custom lens shader for vignette, grain, fisheye and colour fringing.
- cannon-es: a JavaScript physics engine for vehicles, falling debris and collapses.
- Playwright (Python): opens the page in a real browser (Edge or Chrome with the GPU on) and captures every frame as an image.
- ffmpeg: the command-line video and audio tool. It joins the frames into an MP4, cuts and filters the audio (highpass, lowpass and echo for voices behind doors), mixes, normalises loudness and makes the phone-size copy.
- ElevenLabs, or Kokoro (free local text-to-speech), for the narrator.
- faster-whisper: free local speech-to-text with word timestamps. Use it to cut the voice cleanly and to time every caption.
- numpy and Pillow: to check audio levels and make contact sheets of stills.
- Sound: free downloaded sound effects from Mixkit (never synthesized) and a dark cinematic drone or tension bed with no vocals.
</tools>

<build>
1. One HTML page (film . html) with the 3D renderer at 1080x1920 drawn into a 2D canvas that also holds the overlay. A function window . seek (t) draws frame t and must be a pure function of time; every cut, sound and move is keyed to the word times.
2. Stickman. Draw each figure with 2D canvas strokes onto its own texture and put it on a plane that always faces the camera, with an alpha test so it casts a real shadow and slight emissive so it reads in the dark. Pose with joint angles, and walk with 2-bone IK so the planted foot never slides.
3. Physics and cloth. Simulate once at load with a fixed timestep, record the positions, then sample them by time, so every render is identical. Cloth (sheets, curtains, flags) is a verlet particle grid with wall and floor collisions and pinned points you can release.
4. Voice. If you generate one long take, never cut it at the API's character timestamps: they drift and slice words. Transcribe the take with faster-whisper word timestamps, match it to the script, cut only in real silence between lines, and only add pause where the natural one is too short.
5. Captions. Re-transcribe each final line, normalise numbers ("6:42" = "6 42", "AM" = "a m"), align the caption words to what was heard, and snap each word to its real start in the audio. Check that every caption has voice under it within ~120 ms.
6. Render. Playwright steps window . seek through every frame at 30 fps, and ffmpeg encodes a high-quality master, then a phone copy under 30 MB.
7. Mix with ffmpeg: the voice on top, the music about 12-14 dB under it, one sound effect per event, a dip before the big moment, loudness at -14 LUFS, then a scan for dropouts.
</build>

-  is narrow: a normal lens sees very little sideways, so use wider lenses indoors and keep the subject close to the aim point.
- Glass behind a solid frame is invisible: build mirrors and windows as a frame around a real hole.
- Dust spread everywhere reads as stars, so keep it inside light beams.
- Night shots go black after compression, so give each one a cold fill light.
- Fog swallows distant things.
- Never judge a reference or your own render from one frame every few seconds; check motion at the full frame rate.

There is nothing special about this pullback.

Much of the panic surrounding neoclouds, AI capital expenditures, and the sustainability of the infrastructure buildout is simply the market searching for explanations for falling stock prices.

When AI stocks were rising, record capex was evidence of extraordinary demand. When those same stocks started falling, suddenly the same spending became evidence of an impending financial disaster.

One fact with two interpretations that depend entirely on the price action of the market.

Go back to August 1998.

The technology bull market had been running for about three years.Amid fallout from the Asian financial crisis and Russian ruble crisis, earnings expectations were deteriorating, valuations were elevated, and investors were becoming increasingly concerned about unprofitable Internet companies.

On August 6, the New York Times published an article titled "Market Gyrations May Point to Shift in Investor Strategy." One fund manager declared, "Boring is going to outperform sexy."

Investors were supposedly abandoning momentum and speculative technology shares in favor of profitable businesses, balance sheets, dividends, and traditional valuations.

Russia defaulted on its debt. The Asian financial crisis was spreading internationally. The yen carry trade had imploded as the USD plunged 8% against the yen in a single day. US embassies were being bombed. 

President Clinton ordered missile strikes against Afghanistan and Sudan while simultaneously facing a scandal that would result in his impeachment. Major financial institutions suffered enormous losses, and the spectacular collapse of Long-Term Capital Management threatened the stability of the global financial system.

Corporate earnings forecasts were falling. Investors feared a U.S. recession. Many of the same technology companies that had driven the bull market were now leading the decline. Many of them had fallen 40-60% from their 1998 highs.

Even the Federal Reserve's first interest-rate cut on September 29 initially disappointed investors. The Dow fell that day and plunged another 238 points the following session.

The news seemed almost uniformly terrible.
But the market didn't care forever.

After a violent reversal in early October, improving confidence in corporate earnings, Japanese banking reforms, and a surprise emergency Fed cut on October 15 helped restore risk appetite.

By November, the Dow was making new all-time highs. Internet stocks were exploding higher again.

What had looked like the end of the internet trade was, within about a month, actually a correction preceding one of the most extraordinary speculative advances in stock-market history.

In today’s market, Microsoft just reported 48% Azure growth. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled. Meta expects $135–145 billion in capex this year and has announced plans for a potentially record-sized $97.5 billion equity capital raise.

If the market really was that concerned over capex spending, instead of using it as an excuse to explain the pullback, the market would have sold off on the META news.

Anthropic has now filed its IPO registration statement. We have midterm elections approaching, another consequential round of earnings, and a Fed that just held rates steady even as another hike is widely anticipated in December.

There are plenty of potential catalysts over the coming two months.

More importantly, this does not resemble the sentiment backdrop of a speculative bubble climax. Generational bull markets don't die midway through a basing period, but typically after euphoric saturation and a parabolic rally in leading names.

Consensus on AI is deeply divided. Being loudly anti-AI has practically become fashionable. Some AI critics have even built enormous audiences around the idea that the economics of the industry are unsustainable. Plenty of investors seem almost eager to watch the entire trade collapse.

That isn't the sentiment or narrative around which tops are typically made.

The Internet trade didn't end in the panic of 1998. It ended after the extraordinary acceleration of 1999 and early 2000 when being bearish was the market equivalent of wearing a dunce cap.

History never repeats perfectly, and today's rate environment is very different. But I think the resemblance in investor psychology is striking.

I’d be genuinely surprised if we don't have at least one more months-long rally into new highs during this cycle. 

Whether it begins into the midterms, after the elections, around Anthropic's anticipated listing, or following further earnings confirmation, I suspect this correction will eventually look more like an interruption in a generational bull market than the bursting of a "bubble."

The $NDX took four months to bottom in 1998. With the exception of a handful of leaders, most stocks that are holding up have been basing out since the May-July period. We could certainly go lower, but most of the signs point to  another new high before this cycle rolls over. 

However, I’d place the odds of any additional powerful rallies afterward as increasingly unlikely given the fact we are already about to enter the fifth year of this bull market. I'd be careful about buying the dips next year, at least with meaningful size.

What would the writing of superintelligent AI sound like? You might expect it to have the characteristics of good human writing — figurative language, high information density, coining new terms, and punchiness — but dialed up to 11. Well, that’s what Claude did, until Anthropic dialed it back recently because of user complaints. It didn’t sound superintelligent to most of us. Instead, the neuralese writing style sounds like a “stupid person’s idea of a smart person”.

Our response to information density and metaphor-laden writing looks something like the cartoon graph I've drawn. Beyond a point, it completely backfires. The reason human writers don’t overdo it isn’t because they aren’t capable, but because they are aware of the reader’s cognitive burden. One of the hardest skills to learn as a writer is to simulate the reader’s experience.

It’s easy to train AI to mimic mediocre human writing. But optimizing it to be (perceived as) good is really hard, and made much harder by the fact that when everyone uses the same few AI models we get tired of their tics very quickly. Most Claudeisms are individually pretty good. I hate that I can’t use “load bearing” in my writing any more. If it weren’t for AI overuse it would be a neat metaphor.

A broader question is whether most tasks in the economy are like chess, where there is a clear performance metric that can be optimized, or whether they’re like writing, where quality is a multidimensional balancing act without clear training signals beyond human mimicry.

Compaction is a mistake.

When an agent's context fills up, tools like Codex and Claude Code compact it:
1. The model prefills the entire session again
2. It writes a summary of everything so far
3. A new session starts from that summary

I measured this on a real ~400k-token session with Opus 5.5:
→ 38 s and $1.99 when the prompt cache has expired
→ 29 s and $0.17 when it hasn't

And the summary is lossy. The exact error message, the file path, the one number you needed is often gone.

So I do something new for Mainplane

Context retrieval works the other way around. Mainplane keeps the full record of every session as a file. When the context fills up, a new session starts right away with one instruction: "You are continuing session X. Retrieve key context from it as you go."

The agent searches the old session and copies the exact lines it needs, when it needs them.

Same session, same model: 15 s and $0.10 to get back to work. It does not depend on a cache hit, and nothing is paraphrased.

This is the bitter lesson applied to agent memory. Don't hand-design what the model should remember. Give it the full record and good tools, and let it decide.

Mainplane is open source (MIT). Link in the first comment.

CVE-2026-98432 is a good example of something that really concerns me about the future of cybersecurity.

https://t.co/BJbXLKLFNq

For decades, we’ve been building critical infrastructure out of enormous amounts of complex, memory-unsafe code. Humans wrote it. Other humans reviewed it, tested it and searched for vulnerabilities. All working with the same fundamental limitations: limited time, limited attention, incomplete visibility and an inability to reason about every possible interaction and race condition.

And perhaps that’s what protected us to some extent. Attackers had the same limitations as the people developing and defending these systems.

A vulnerability could remain undiscovered for 11 years, even in such a widely used component.

Now AI is changing that balance.

The ability to inspect code, identify subtle weaknesses and develop working exploits is becoming less dependent on a small number of highly skilled researchers. These activities can increasingly be scaled with compute, automated testing and tokens.

And that’s what worries me about the next few years.

We’ve accumulated decades of complex, memory-unsafe code in operating systems, network services, applications and libraries. Much of it has never been assessed with anything close to the capabilities that are now becoming available.

We may have massively overestimated the security of our software simply because the people looking for vulnerabilities were as limited as the people who introduced them.

That balance is breaking down, and I don’t think we’re prepared for what follows.

wtf is an agent harness.

An agent is a model plus a harness.

Model reads the context and picks the next action. The harness is all the code that turns that choice into work.

Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are all harnesses.

8 common parts every agent harness shares:

1. The loop
• Sends the context to the model and runs whatever tools it asks for
• Feeds the results back in for the next step
• Decides when the task is finished

2. Tools and sandbox
• Give the model a terminal, files, a browser and your connected apps
• Run every task inside its own isolated computer
• Keep the damage from a bad command inside the sandbox

3. Subagents
• Take side tasks off the main agent and run them in parallel
• Start each one with a fresh context window
• Send back only a short summary, so the main context stays clean

4. Context management
• Decides what the model sees on every turn
• Loads skills and files only when the task needs them
• Summarizes old history before the context window fills up

5. Memory
• Stores progress notes, git history and skills on disk
• Lets a new session read what the last one did
• Picks the work up where it stopped

6. Guardrails
• Hold risky actions like emails, payments and deletes for your approval
• Keep real credentials outside the sandbox
• Give a prompt injection no credentials to steal

7. Verification
• Stops the agent from handing you a summary that only sounds finished
• Runs tests, browser checks or a separate grader first
• Lets the agent call the task done only after those 
checks pass

8. Observability
• Traces every model call and tool call
• Spots the agent repeating the same failed edit
• Pushes it to try a different approach

follow @Saboo_Shubham_ for more on Agent Harness.

Okay, let's do this.

Isabelle, Lean, and Rocq (formerly Coq*) are theorem provers. They are meant to prove mathematical theorems. We use them for formal verification by either 1) translating a program to the theorem prover (risking a translation error) or 2) using a language built into the theorem prover that extracts into a working binary.

Fizzbee, TLA+, Spin, Alloy, Quint, and P are specification languages. They are meant for checking high-level blueprints of programs. After checking the blueprint, you still need to make sure your program matches it, which is a hard problem.

Specification languages differ in what they make easy to express. P, Spin, and Fizzbee are designed to be closer to the code implementations. P looks like interacting state machines, Spin looks like C with CSP, Fizzbee looks like a dialect of Python. It's easier to use a codelike specification language and refine it to code, but you can't do as much with it.

Alloy, TLA+, and Quint are more abstract. Alloy looks like a bunch of algebraic relationships, TLA+ is a much of logical formula, and Quint is a programmer-oriented (and statically typed) condensation of TLA+. Abstract modeling languages are harder to get started with and harder to represent things, but you can represent a wider class of systems with them.

I believe UPPAAL is a specification language for realtime systems. This is a field I have no experience in. It seems a graphical language, though, which would make LLM-assistance difficult.

Dafny is a verifiable programming language. It has regular programming language features, but also a bunch of features to express and prove properties of the program. It uses SMT solvers to actually prove the properties, meaning you don't need to learn a proof language (though you need to learn to cajole the solver). Dafny is probably the easiest thing on your list to get started with, but also the least likely to meet any weirder needs you might have.

I don't know what Ivy is but some cursory Kagiing suggests it falls in the specification language category.

Some other things @spin_lock_init didn't mention:

- Other theorem provers: Agda, Metamath
- Other abstract specification languages: mcrl2, NuXMV, Event-B
- Other verifiable programming languages: Idris, F*, Whiley
- There's also using a verifiable subset of a language, like Verus for Rust or SPARK for Ada.

So, what you need to pick depends on what you want to do.

You'll get the maximum power with a theorem prover. Lean is the de facto language for vibeproving, but Anthropic recently published a post about vibeproving in Rocq so YMMV.

If you want to make abstract models of software systems, go for a specification language. Which you choose depends on a lot of factors. If your system can be represented as lots of simple communicating state machines over a network, try P. Spin, I believe, is close to simple C/Go with a network and channels. I have never used Fizzbee.

Alloy is good for domain modeling, but struggles with really complicated temporal actions, nested data structures, and largish numbers. Also AIs aren't to good at it (last I checked, in March). Runs fast and makes good visualizations though.

TLA+ and Quint are for modeling complex temporal systems. I'm partial to TLA+ but know a lot of people who say Quint is easier to get into.

Note P, Fizzbee, and Quint all claim to have features for testing a codebase against a spec. I can't vouch for any of them, though. None of the languages I mentioned (except maybe NuXMV?) are particularly good at modeling sequential, deterministic algorithms.

Use Dafny if you need to just write a verified program and don't care which language it's in. I don't think other verifiable programming languages are as user-friendly for the time being. Consider a verified subset if you already know a language and want to just augment it with more correctness.

You may need other, more exotic tools depending on your particular needs. Regardless of the above advice, don't be afraid to use the wrong tool for the job. If you vibe well with a language, and you achieve good LLM-sympathy with it, you'll be able to go farther than using a "right tool" you don't like.
